sections.heading: What Is Low-E Glass and Why Does It Matter for Alexandria Properties?
sections.body: Low-E, or low-emissivity, glass is manufactured with a microscopic metallic coating that reflects infrared and ultraviolet light while still allowing visible light to pass through. This coating reduces the amount of heat that transfers through the glass in both directions — keeping interiors cooler in summer and warmer in winter. For Alexandria properties, where summers can be intensely humid and winters bring sharp temperature drops, this performance characteristic is especially relevant. Commercial buildings near King Street and multifamily properties throughout Del Ray and Rosemont deal with occupant comfort and operational costs year-round. Low-E glass addresses these concerns by improving thermal performance at the window or door unit itself. It also helps reduce UV-related fading of interior furnishings, flooring, and merchandise — a practical benefit for retail storefronts and office spaces alike. Whether you are upgrading an existing building or specifying glazing for a renovation project, Low-E glass is one of the most widely adopted solutions for improving window and door performance in the region.

sections.heading: Low-E Glass Options: Coatings, Configurations, and What to Expect
sections.body: Not all Low-E glass is the same. The performance of a Low-E unit depends on the type of coating used, where the coating is positioned within the insulated glass unit, and whether the unit uses one or two air spaces. Some coatings are designed primarily to block solar heat gain — well suited for south- and west-facing exposures that receive direct sun. Others are engineered to retain interior heat, making them a better fit for north-facing elevations or climates with cold winters. During our consultation process, we discuss the orientation of your windows or doors, the climate conditions specific to your building or home, and your overall goals. We work with reputable glass suppliers to source units that meet the performance specifications appropriate for your project. We can also advise on gas fills such as argon, which are commonly used in conjunction with Low-E coatings to further improve the thermal performance of insulated glass units. Our goal is to match the right product to each specific application.

faq.q: How long does Low-E glass installation typically take?
faq.a: The timeline depends on the scope of the project. A single residential window or door replacement can often be completed in a few hours once the glass unit is fabricated and on hand. Larger commercial projects involving multiple units or custom sizes may take longer due to fabrication lead times and coordination with building occupants. We provide project-specific timelines during the estimate process so you know what to expect before work begins.

faq.q: Can Low-E glass be installed in existing window and door frames?
faq.a: In many cases, yes. We fabricate Low-E insulated glass units to fit existing frames, which allows the upgrade to happen without replacing the entire window or door assembly. This is a common and cost-effective approach for both residential and commercial properties. However, if the existing frame is damaged, warped, or structurally compromised, full replacement may be the more practical option. We assess each situation individually and give you an honest recommendation.

faq.q: Does Low-E glass look different from standard glass?
faq.a: Low-E glass has a very slight tint or reflectivity depending on the specific coating used, but in most applications it is not noticeably different in appearance from standard clear glass. Some coatings may have a subtle blue or green cast when viewed at certain angles. We can show you samples and discuss the visual characteristics of the specific products we recommend for your project so there are no surprises after installation.
